claim: In uncertain environments, seeking information about alternative choice options is essential for adaptive learning and decision-making.
source: In uncertain environments, seeking information about alternative choice options is essential for adaptive learning and decision-making.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research context.

claim: Information seeking is usually confounded with changes-of-mind about the reliability of the preferred option.
source: However, information seeking is usually confounded with changes-of-mind about the reliability of the preferred option.
evidence: This statement identifies a problem in the existing literature that the study addresses.

claim: Information seeking requires control over which option to sample.
source: Here, we exploited the fact that information seeking requires control over which option to sample to isolate its behavioral and neurophysiological signatures.
evidence: This is a key theoretical premise of the study design.

claim: Changes-of-mind occurring with control require more evidence against the current option.
source: We found that changes-of-mind occurring with control require more evidence against the current option, are associated with reduced confidence, but are nevertheless more likely to be confirmed on the next decision.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Changes-of-mind occurring with control are associated with reduced confidence.
source: We found that changes-of-mind occurring with control require more evidence against the current option, are associated with reduced confidence, but are nevertheless more likely to be confirmed on the next decision.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Changes-of-mind occurring with control are more likely to be confirmed on the next decision.
source: We found that changes-of-mind occurring with control require more evidence against the current option, are associated with reduced confidence, but are nevertheless more likely to be confirmed on the next decision.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Changes-of-mind with control are preceded by stronger activation of the dorsal attention network in magnetoencephalography.
source: Multimodal neurophysiological recordings showed that these changes-of-mind are preceded by stronger activation of the dorsal attention network in magnetoencephalography, and followed by increased pupil-linked arousal during the presentation of decision outcomes.
evidence: This is a primary neurophysiological finding reported in the abstract and supported by MEG data in Figure 6.

claim: Changes-of-mind with control are followed by increased pupil-linked arousal during the presentation of decision outcomes.
source: Multimodal neurophysiological recordings showed that these changes-of-mind are preceded by stronger activation of the dorsal attention network in magnetoencephalography, and followed by increased pupil-linked arousal during the presentation of decision outcomes.
evidence: This is a primary neurophysiological finding reported in the abstract and supported by pupillometry data in Figure 7.

claim: Information seeking increases the saliency of evidence perceived as the direct consequence of one's own actions.
source: Together, these findings indicate that information seeking increases the saliency of evidence perceived as the direct consequence of one's own actions.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral and neurophysiological findings.

claim: The inference process of forming and revising uncertain beliefs through information sampling has been extensively studied using two main classes of decision tasks.
source: This inference process has been extensively studied using two main classes of decision tasks (Bartolo and Averbeck, 2021; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In passive sampling tasks, participants are observers who sample information over which they have no control.
source: In passive sampling tasks, participants are observers who sample information over which they have no control (Murphy et al., 2016; van den Berg et al., 2016; Zylberberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Active sampling tasks let participants choose which source of information to sample from.
source: By contrast, active sampling tasks let participants choose which source of information to sample from Charpentier et al., 2018; Gureckis and Markant, 2012; Markant and Gureckis, 2014.
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Unlike passive sampling, active sampling provides participants with control over which source of information to sample from.
source: Critically, unlike passive sampling, active sampling provides participants with control over which source of information to sample from, even if the information itself (about the new movie) can be exactly the same in both cases.
evidence: This is a key distinction made by the authors to motivate their experimental design.

claim: Low confidence in current beliefs has been shown to predict changes-of-mind.
source: Low confidence in current beliefs has been shown to predict changes-of-mind (Balsdon et al., 2020; Folke et al., 2016) and allows for the flexible adaptation of behavioral strategies even when external feedback is unavailable (Desender et al., 2018; Desender et al., 2019; Fleming et al., 2018; Rollwage et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Low confidence allows for the flexible adaptation of behavioral strategies even when external feedback is unavailable.
source: Low confidence in current beliefs has been shown to predict changes-of-mind (Balsdon et al., 2020; Folke et al., 2016) and allows for the flexible adaptation of behavioral strategies even when external feedback is unavailable (Desender et al., 2018; Desender et al., 2019; Fleming et al., 2018; Rollwage et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Information seeking has been mostly studied using 'exploration-exploitation' dilemmas.
source: Information seeking has been mostly studied using 'exploration-exploitation' dilemmas (Costa et al., 2019; Daw et al., 2006), where it is confounded with changes-of-mind about the reliability of the current behavioral strategy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In exploration-exploitation paradigms, information seeking is confounded with changes-of-mind about the reliability of the current behavioral strategy.
source: Information seeking has been mostly studied using 'exploration-exploitation' dilemmas (Costa et al., 2019; Daw et al., 2006), where it is confounded with changes-of-mind about the reliability of the current behavioral strategy.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in previous research that the current study addresses.

claim: Exploration is known to be associated with larger pupil-linked arousal.
source: At the neurophysiological level, exploration is known to be associated with larger pupil-linked arousal (Jepma and Nieuwenhuis, 2011) and increased activity in lateral prefrontal regions in electroencephalographic (EEG) and blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) activity (Donoso et al., 2014; Tzovara et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological research.

claim: Exploration is known to be associated with increased activity in lateral prefrontal regions in electroencephalographic (EEG) and blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) activity.
source: At the neurophysiological level, exploration is known to be associated with larger pupil-linked arousal (Jepma and Nieuwenhuis, 2011) and increased activity in lateral prefrontal regions in electroencephalographic (EEG) and blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) activity (Donoso et al., 2014; Tzovara et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological research.

claim: No study has directly manipulated control over evidence sampling in otherwise aligned experimental conditions.
source: To date, no study has directly manipulated control over evidence sampling in otherwise aligned experimental conditions.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study fills.

claim: Participants were slower to adapt after a reversal in the C+ condition.
source: We found that participants were slower to adapt after a reversal in the C+ condition, with psychometric fits indicating a higher reversal time constant in this controllable condition (t32 = 5.0, p=1.95 × 10–5; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Participants reached a higher asymptotic reversal rate in the C+ condition.
source: Participants also reached a higher asymptotic reversal rate in the C+ condition (t32 = 6.3, p=4.0 × 10–7; Figure 2B), replicating earlier findings (Weiss et al., 2021).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis, shown in Figure 2B, and replicates previous work.

claim: Participants' confidence decreased after a reversal in both conditions.
source: As expected, participants' confidence decreased after a reversal in both conditions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Confidence decreased more sharply in the C+ condition.
source: However, confidence decreased more sharply in the C+ (Figure 2D), an observation confirmed by psychometric fits of a confidence 'drop' parameter (t32 = 3.59, p=0.0011; see 'Methods').
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The confidence time constant characterizing the slope of confidence increase after a reversal was slightly higher in the C+ condition.
source: In addition, the confidence time constant characterizing the slope of confidence increase after a reversal was slightly higher in the C+ condition (paired t-test, t32 = −1.9, p=0.064; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = −2.65, p=0.008) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Participants switched their category choice more often in the C- (32% of trials) than in the C+ (22% of trials) condition.
source: We then established that participants switched their category choice more often in the C- (32% of trials) than in the C+ (22% of trials) condition (t32 = 8.64, p=7.2 × 10–10).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Participants' choice accuracy was slightly higher in the C+ (81.9% correct) than in the C- (78.4% correct) condition.
source: Participants' choice accuracy was slightly higher in the C+ (81.9% correct) than in the C- (78.4% correct) condition (t32 = −4.9, p=2.6 × 10–5).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Response times (RTs) on repeat decisions were similar between C- and C+ conditions.
source: Moreover, response times (RTs) on repeat decisions were similar between C- (mean = 693.2 ms, SEM = 55.4 ms, median = 608.9 ms) and C+ (mean = 677.5 ms, SEM = 45.2 ms, median = 626.7 ms) conditions (t32 = −1.52, p=0.14, BF10 = 0.531).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis including Bayesian analysis.

claim: Participants needed more evidence against their previous decision for switching in the C+ condition.
source: Crucially, psychometric fits revealed a difference in the point of subjective equivalence (choice-PSE) between conditions (t32 = −7.83, p=6.2 × 10–9; Figure 2F). The choice-PSE parameter reflects the amount of evidence required for a participant to switch away from their previous choice more often than repeat it. This difference means that participants needed more evidence against their previous decision for switching in the C+ condition.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Participants' sensitivity to the available objective evidence was not significantly different across conditions.
source: In contrast, participants' sensitivity to the available objective evidence was not significantly different across conditions (t32 = 1.09, p=0.28, BF10 = 0.323; Figure 2F).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis including Bayesian analysis and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Participants were considerably less confident in their choices following inconsistent evidence in the C+ condition.
source: By contrast, participants were considerably less confident in their choices following inconsistent evidence in the C+ condition (Figure 2G).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Participants needed more inconsistent evidence to be equally confident in switch and repeat decisions in the C+ condition.
source: We found a significant confidence-PSE difference between conditions (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z = −2.89, p=0.0038; Figure 2H), indicating that participants needed more inconsistent evidence to be equally confident in switch and repeat decisions in the C+ condition.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The sensitivity of confidence reports to evidence (slope) was smaller in the C+ than in the C- condition on switch decisions.
source: We also found that the sensitivity of confidence reports to evidence (slope) was smaller in the C+ than in the C- condition on switch decisions (t32 = 5.1, p=1.6 × 10–5; Figure 2H).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: There was no difference in reversal time constant between retrospective and prospective conditions.
source: Psychometric analyses of behavior indicate no difference in reversal time constant between retrospective and prospective conditions (t24 = −0.016, p=0.98, BF10 = 0.21) and a small difference in asymptotic reversal rate (t24 = 2.2, p=0.038, BF10 = 1.59).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis including Bayesian analysis.

claim: There was no difference in choice-PSE between retrospective and prospective conditions.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in choice-PSE (t24 = −1.67, p=0.11, BF10 = 0.70) or sensitivity to evidence (t24 = 1.2, p=0.25, BF10 = 0.39) between retrospective and prospective conditions (see Weiss et al., 2021 for a detailed analysis).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis including Bayesian analysis and references previous work.

claim: Participants were generally less confident when they switched than when they repeated their previous response.
source: Following a switch decision, we found that participants were generally less confident when they switched than when they repeated their previous response (main effect of response type, F1,32 = 55.8, p=1.7 × 10–8), and were also less confident in the C+ compared to the C- condition (main effect of condition, F1,32 = 17.9, p=0.00018; Figure 3A).
evidence: This finding is supported by ANOVA analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant interaction between response type and condition for confidence.
source: We further identified a significant interaction between response type and condition (F1,32 = 18.9, p=0.00014), indicating a more pronounced decrease in confidence on switch decisions in the C+ compared to the C- condition.
evidence: This finding is supported by ANOVA analysis.

claim: After a switch decision, participants were less willing to go back to their previous response in the C+ condition, with 72.7% of switches being confirmed, but only 58.9% in the C- condition.
source: We found that after a switch decision participants were less willing to go back to their previous response in the C+ condition, with 72.7% of switches being confirmed, but only 58.9% in the C- condition (t32 = −8.19, p=2.4 × 10–9).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Participants were more confident on trials in which switch decisions were confirmed compared to aborted.
source: Moreover, participants were more confident on trials in which switch decisions were confirmed compared to aborted (F1,32 = 10.3, p=0.0030), and more confident in the C- than in the C+ condition (F1,32 = 20.6, p=0.0001), with an interaction between these factors (F1,32 = 10.7, p=0.0026), due to participants' confidence decreasing on aborted switches as compared to confirmed switches in the C+ condition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This finding is supported by ANOVA analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Participants confirmed their switch more often when it was made with high confidence.
source: We found a main effect of confidence on the fraction of switches confirmed (F1,27 = 30.4, p=7.8 × 10–6), meaning that participants confirmed their switch more often when it was made with high confidence.
evidence: This finding is supported by ANOVA analysis.

claim: Switch decisions were more often confirmed in the C+ condition.
source: Switch decisions were more often confirmed in the C+ condition (F1,27 = 47.8, p=1.98 × 10–7), consistent with a higher flexibility of responses in the C- condition, without an interaction between confidence and condition (F1,27 = 0.093, p=0.76).
evidence: This finding is supported by ANOVA analysis.

claim: There was a similar amount of inference noise between conditions.
source: We observed a similar amount of inference noise between conditions (t32 = 1.45, p=0.16), indicating that evidence was integrated equally well across conditions, in line with psychometric results (Figure 2).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters and is consistent with behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: There was a lower perceived hazard rate in the C+ relative to the C- condition.
source: We found a lower perceived hazard rate in the C+ relative to the C- condition (t32 = 7.46, p=1.7 × 10–8), indicating that participants perceived the environment as less volatile when being in control (Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a lower confidence threshold in the C- condition, which corresponds to more high-confident responses, compared to the C+ condition.
source: In line with model-free analyses indicating a difference in the fraction of high-confidence responses between conditions, we found a lower confidence threshold in the C- condition, which corresponds to more high-confident responses, compared to the C+ condition (t32 = −4.3, p=1.3 × 10–4), together with no difference in metacognitive noise (t32 = −0.29, p=0.76), or confidence gain for switch trials (t32 = 0.10, p=0.92; Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the C- condition, more evidence was required to switch away from the current best option following a repeat compared to a switch trial.
source: For human choices in the C- condition, we found a higher PSE following a repeat compared to a switch trial, indicating that more evidence was required to switch away from the current best option (t32 = 3.2, p=0.0033), whereas in the C+ condition, PSEs were similar after repeat and switch trials (t32 = 0.08, p=0.93; Figure 5A, bars).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the C+ condition, participants required more evidence to switch back following a change-of-mind, deviating from model predictions.
source: This deviation from model predictions indicates that participants required more evidence to switch back following a change-of-mind in the controllable C+ condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the discrepancy between model and human data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The switch effect occurred earlier in the occipital cluster than in the frontal cluster.
source: Inspecting time courses of the 'repeat minus switch' contrast (hereafter, 'switch effect'; Figure 6B) revealed that the switch effect occurred earlier in the occipital cluster (time from trial onset, occipital: 1.450 ± 0.229 s, frontal: 2.099 ± 0.243 s, jackknifed mean ± SEM; jackknifed t23 = 3.1, p=0.005) and peaked before the response probe onset (time from probe onset, occipital: –0.393 ± 0.028 s; jackknifed t23 = −14.2, p<0.001).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The switch effect started later and peaked after the probe onset in the frontal cluster.
source: In contrast, the switch effect started later and peaked after the probe onset (+0.958 ± 0.032 s; jackknifed t23 = 29.6, p<0.001) in the frontal cluster (Figure 6B).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The occipital switch effect was larger than the frontal effect before the response probe onset.
source: The occipital switch effect was larger than the frontal effect before the response probe onset (during the sequence, peak t23 = 6.0, cluster-level p<0.001), whereas the frontal effect was larger than the occipital effect after the probe onset (during and after the response, peak t23 = 7.5, cluster-level p<0.001; Figure 6C).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the occipital cluster, the switch effect was larger in the C+ than the C- condition.
source: In the occipital cluster (Figure 6D), the switch effect was larger in the C+ than the C- condition (peak t23 = 6.2, cluster-level p<0.001), with the largest difference just before probe onset (Figure 6E, see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B for the raw effects).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: In the occipital cluster, there was no significant difference between conditions on repeat trials but a significant one on switch trials.
source: We found no significant difference between conditions on repeat trials (t23 = 0.6, p=0.528) but a significant one on switch trials (t23 = 3.9, p<0.001) (Figure 6F) (interaction: F1,23 = 40.7, p<0.001; Figure 6E).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: The frontal cluster featured a larger (and longer) switch effect in the C+ than the C- condition.
source: The frontal cluster (Figure 6G) featured a larger (and longer) switch effect in the C+ than the C- condition (peak t23 = 4.4, cluster-level p<0.001), with the largest difference just after probe onset (Figure 6H, see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D for the raw effects).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: In the frontal cluster, there was no significant difference between conditions on repeat trials but a significant one on switch trials.
source: As for the occipital cluster, we found no significant difference between conditions on repeat trials (t23 = 1.1, p=0.27), but a significant one on switch trials (t23 = 4.1, p<.001) (Figure 6I) (interaction: F1,23 = 24.6, p<0.001; Figure 6H).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of MEG data and shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: In both MEG clusters, switch decisions are driving the differences between conditions.
source: Thus, in both clusters, switch decisions are driving the differences between conditions.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: There was no difference in motor lateralization between conditions at a liberal sample-wise threshold p<0.05.
source: We found no difference in motor lateralization between conditions at a liberal sample-wise threshold p<0.05. This suggests that the effects described above are truly about changes-of-mind, not the preparation of a response switch (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is supported by analysis of motor lateralization shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the occipital cluster, there were significant correlations between the alpha effect and the choice-PSE across participants in both the C- and C+ conditions.
source: In the occipital cluster, we found significant correlations between the alpha effect and the choice-PSE across participants in the C- (ρ = 0.496, p=0.013) and C+ (ρ = 0.585, p=0.002) condition.
evidence: This finding is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: In the frontal cluster, the correlations between alpha effect and choice-PSE were similar in direction but not statistically significant.
source: In the frontal cluster, however, the direction of correlations was similar, but these effects were not statistically significant (C- condition: ρ = 0.311, p=0.137; C+ condition: ρ = 0.357, p=0.086).
evidence: This finding is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: In both conditions, pupil dilation increased slightly before, but mainly after probe onset, with a first peak around 1 s after probe onset and a second peak corresponding to the next trial.
source: In both conditions, pupil dilation increased slightly before, but mainly after probe onset, with a first peak around 1 s after probe onset and a second peak corresponding to the next trial (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F for raw effects).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Pupil dilation was similar across conditions on repeat trials but was larger in the C+ than in the C- condition on switch trials.
source: Within this time window, pupil dilation was similar across conditions on repeat trials (t30 = 1.37, p=0.18), but was larger in the C+ than in the C- condition on switch trials (t30 = −5.48, p=5.94 × 10–6).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of pupillometry data.

claim: The IBI increased before probe onset and slowly decreased thereafter.
source: In both conditions, the IBI increased before probe onset and slowly decreased thereafter (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H for raw effects), a dynamic comparable to that of the alpha-band response suppression observed in MEG.
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The IBI increase was larger on switch than on repeat trials in both conditions.
source: This increase was larger on switch than on repeat trials (C-: t23 = 3.8, p<0.001; C+: t23 = 6.5, p<0.001; Figure 7C), an effect that was more pronounced in the C+ than in the C- condition (main effect of condition: F1,23 = 12.6, p=0.002; main effect of response type: F1,23 = 34.8, p<0.001; interaction response type and condition: F1,23 = 5.8, p=0.024; Figure 7D).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: The alpha-band effects associated with switch responses arose earlier for long compared to short sequences across conditions, both in the occipital and frontal clusters.
source: We observed that the alpha-band effects associated with switch responses arose earlier for long compared to short sequences across conditions, both in the occipital (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) and frontal (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B) clusters (main effect of sequence length, occipital: peak F1,23 = 25.1, cluster-level p<0.001; frontal: peak F1,23 = 17.7, cluster-level p<0.001).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Pupil dilation did not differ significantly across the two sequence length groups.
source: In contrast, pupil dilation did not differ significantly across the two sequence length groups. In both conditions, pupil dilation on changes-of-mind increased only after the response (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The IBI revealed dynamics comparable to those of the alpha-band suppression, with differences between short and long sequences restricted to before the probe onset.
source: Finally, the IBI revealed dynamics comparable to those of the alpha-band suppression, with differences between short and long sequences restricted to before the probe onset (main effect of sequence length: peak F1,23 = 10.4, cluster-level p<0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Absolute prior beliefs were stronger on a repeat than on a switch trial and higher in the C+ than in the C- condition.
source: As expected, we found that absolute prior beliefs were stronger on a repeat than on a switch trial (F1,32 = 59.02, p=9.3 × 10–9) and higher than in the C+ than in the C- condition (F1,32 = 72.3, p=1.0 × 10–9), in line with a lower perceived hazard rate found in the C+ condition, with an interaction between response type and condition (F1,32 = 11.7, p=0.0017).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of model-derived variables.

claim: Evidence direction was strongly positive on repeat decisions and negative on switch decisions, an effect that was more pronounced in the C+ than in the C- condition.
source: We also established that evidence direction strongly was positive (resp. negative) on repeat (resp. switch) decisions (F1,32 = 7527.9, p<1 × 10–11), an effect that was more pronounced in the C+ than in the C- condition (F1,32 = 52.5, p=3.1 × 10–8) with an interaction between response type and condition (F1,32 = 5.59, p=0.024).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of model-derived variables.

claim: In the occipital cluster, when controlling for the effects of both model variables, the C- switch effect disappears before probe onset, but remains afterward, while the C+ switch effect remained present, albeit smaller, before and after probe onset.
source: In the occipital cluster, when controlling for the effects of both model variables, the C- switch effect disappears before probe onset, but remains afterward. By contrast, the C+ switch effect remained present, albeit smaller, before and after probe onset (residual variance, Figure 8B).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 8B after controlling for model variables.

claim: The difference in switch effect in the occipital cluster remained significant when accounting for prior belief and decision evidence.
source: Importantly, the difference in switch effect remained significant when accounting for these two model variables (interaction response type and condition: F1,23 = 21.9, p<0.001), meaning that the original difference between conditions (Figure 6) cannot be explained away by different prior beliefs or decision evidence.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis after controlling for model variables.

claim: In the frontal cluster, all effects fully remained after controlling for prior belief and decision evidence.
source: In the frontal cluster, all effects again fully remained after controlling for prior belief and decision evidence (interaction response type and condition: F1,23 = 18.0, p<0.001; residual variance, Figure 8B).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In pupil dilation, when controlling for the effects of both variables, the switch effect remained larger in the C+ than in the C- condition.
source: Likewise, in pupil dilation, when controlling for the effects of both variables, the switch effect remained larger in the C+ than in the C- condition (interaction response type and condition: F1,30 = 8.9, p=0.005) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: When controlling for prior belief and evidence direction, the switch effect in cardiac IBI remained in both conditions, albeit smaller, but the difference between conditions was no longer significant.
source: When controlling for both variables, the switch effect remained in both conditions, albeit smaller, but the difference between conditions was no longer significant, indicating that evidence direction was driving the switch effect observed in cardiac IBI (compare Figure 7C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1) (interaction response type and condition: F1,23 = 0.3, p=0.57).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and comparison between Figure 7C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Participants with obsessive-compulsive disorder typically need to gather more evidence before committing to a decision.
source: For instance, participants with obsessive-compulsive disorder typically need to gather more evidence before committing to a decision, while participants with schizophrenia present an inflated sense of agency associated with an inability to accurately update these representations (Metcalfe et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Participants with schizophrenia present an inflated sense of agency associated with an inability to accurately update these representations.
source: For instance, participants with obsessive-compulsive disorder typically need to gather more evidence before committing to a decision, while participants with schizophrenia present an inflated sense of agency associated with an inability to accurately update these representations (Metcalfe et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Stimuli were oriented bars drawn from either of two categories (orange and blue), whose means are orthogonal to each other.
source: Stimuli were oriented bars drawn from either of two categories (orange and blue), whose means are orthogonal to each other.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli shown in Figure 1D.

claim: On each trial, a sequence of 2, 4, 6, or 8 stimuli was drawn from a von Mises probability distribution centered on either category with a concentration of 0.5.
source: On each trial, a sequence of 2, 4, 6, or 8 stimuli was drawn from a von Mises probability distribution centered on either category with a concentration of 0.5 and presented to participants for making a decision about category of origin at the end of the sequence (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of stimuli per sequence was drawn from a uniform distribution and pseudo-randomized across trials.
source: The number of stimuli per sequence was drawn from a uniform distribution and pseudo-randomized across trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Stimuli were displayed at an average rate of 2 Hz with an inter-stimulus interval of 500 ± 50 ms.
source: Stimuli were displayed at an average rate of 2 Hz with an inter-stimulus interval of 500 ± 50 ms.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The last stimulus of each sequence was followed by a longer delay of 1000 ± 50 ms, before participants were probed for their response.
source: The last stimulus of each sequence was followed by a longer delay of 1000 ± 50 ms, before participants were probed for their response.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants completed a total of 576 trials divided into blocks of 72 trials.
source: Participants completed a total of 576 trials divided into blocks of 72 trials (72 sequences).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Episode duration was sampled pseudo-randomly from a truncated exponential probability distribution (between 4 and 24 trials), resulting in a near-constant hazard rate in each block.
source: Episode duration was sampled pseudo-randomly from a truncated exponential probability distribution (between 4 and 24 trials), resulting in a near-constant hazard rate in each block.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The order of condition administration was counterbalanced pseudo-randomly across participants.
source: The order of condition administration was also counterbalanced pseudo-randomly across participants (C-/C+/C-/C+ for odd-numbered subjects, C+/C-/C+/C- for even-numbered subjects).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: 17 participants were originally recruited for Experiment 1, with one excluded for aborting the experiment and one for performing at chance level, leaving 15 participants for behavioral analyses.
source: Experiment 1: 17 participants were originally recruited in February–March 2016. One participant was excluded for aborting the experiment before the end and one for performing at chance level, leaving 15 participants for behavioral analyses.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: 20 participants were initially recruited for Experiment 2, with two excluded for performing at chance level, leaving 18 participants for behavioral analyses.
source: Experiment 2: 20 participants were initially recruited in November–December 2016 and in March–May 2017. Two participants were excluded for performing at chance level, leaving 18 participants for behavioral analyses.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: 30 participants were initially recruited for Experiment 3, with four excluded for performing at chance level and one for aborting the experiment, leaving 25 participants for behavioral analyses.
source: Experiment 3: 30 participants were initially recruited in March 2019. Four participants were excluded for performing at chance level and one participant aborted the experiment before the end, leaving 25 participants for behavioral analyses.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: 24 participants were tested in Experiment 4.
source: Experiment 4: 24 participants were tested in September–November 2015, whose behavior is described in Weiss et al., 2021.
evidence: This describes the participant sample and references previous work.

claim: The study was approved by the Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile-de-France VI, ID RCB: 2007-A01125-48, 2017-A01778-45.
source: The study was approved by the Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile-de-France VI, ID RCB: 2007-A01125-48, 2017-A01778-45.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: MEG data were recorded using a whole-head Elekta Neuromag TRIUX system composed of 204 planar gradiometers and 102 magnetometers using a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz.
source: As reported in our previous study (Experiment 4, Weiss et al., 2021), we recorded MEG data using a whole-head Elekta Neuromag TRIUX system (Elekta Instrument AB, Stockholm, Sweden) composed of 204 planar gradiometers and 102 magnetometers using a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the MEG recording setup.

claim: The movement of HPI coils between blocks remained small (mean: 2.3 mm) and was similar across blocks and across conditions.
source: The movement of HPI coils between blocks remained small (mean: 2.3 mm) was similar across blocks and across conditions (t23 = 1.6, p=0.128).
evidence: This describes quality control for MEG recordings.

claim: The spectral power of band-limited MEG oscillations between 8 and 16 Hz was estimated using the 'multitapering' time-frequency transform implemented in FieldTrip.
source: The spectral power of band-limited MEG oscillations between 8 and 16 Hz was estimated using the 'multitapering' time-frequency transform implemented in FieldTrip (Oostenveld et al., 2011) (Slepian tapers, eight cycles and three tapers per window, corresponding to a frequency smoothing of 25%), in two distinct time windows time-locked either to trial onset (from to 0 to +4s from trial onset) or to probe onset (from –4 to +4s from probe onset).
evidence: This describes the MEG analysis method with citation to the software used.

claim: Pupil dilation was measured at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz in Experiments 1 and 2.
source: To analyze physiological correlates of uncertainty across conditions, we measured pupil dilation at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz in Experiments 1 and 2.
evidence: This describes the pupillometry recording setup.

claim: Two participants were excluded from pupillometry analyses due to more than 50% of low-quality data due to blinks.
source: We excluded from the analyses blocks in which participants had more than 50% of low-quality data due to blinks (N = 2 participants excluded from these analyses).
evidence: This describes quality control for pupillometry data.

claim: The model was fitted using a Bayesian Adaptive Direct Search (BADS) with 100 validation samples.
source: We fitted the model using a Bayesian Adaptive Direct Search (BADS) with 100 validation samples that provides point estimates for each parameter (Acerbi and Ma, 2017).
evidence: This describes the model fitting procedure with citation.

claim: All correlations between generative and recovered parameters were high (all ρ>0.78, all p<10–14).
source: All correlations between generative and recovered parameters were high (all ρ>0.78, all p<10–14), while other correlations were low as indicated in a confusion matrix (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the parameter recovery validation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no order effects for any of the best-fitting parameters.
source: Likewise, there were no order effects for any of the best-fitting parameters (for all comparisons between conditions, all t31 < 1.85, all p>0.074).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Mean accuracy and mean confidence were similar across order groups.
source: Mean accuracy and mean confidence were similar across order groups (independent t-tests, all t31 < −1.2, all p>0.23).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between inference noise and hazard rate.
source: We found a significant negative correlation between inference noise and hazard rate (ρ = −0.51, p=0.0025), in line with a previously reported trade-off between these two sources of variability (Weiss et al., 2021).
evidence: This finding is supported by correlation analysis and references previous work.

claim: There was a borderline correlation between confidence threshold and hazard rate.
source: We also found a borderline correlation between confidence threshold and hazard rate (ρ = −0.36, p=0.0409).
evidence: This finding is supported by correlation analysis.
